audio.t: Good afternoon, everyone. As your capstone coordinator, I want to explain how the showcase will be judged. This year we've invited five judges: three professors from our department and two engineers from local companies. Each judge will visit every booth and give scores in three areas: technical quality, teamwork, and communication.

Communication is where many teams lose points. The judges are not looking for a long lecture. They want you to explain the problem you solved, show how your product works, and answer questions clearly. Practice a two-minute summary that everyone on your team can give, because the judges may ask any member to speak.

The top three teams will receive prize money, and the winning team will represent our university at the national competition in March. Also, remember that the showcase counts for thirty percent of your final grade, so even if you don't win, your effort matters. Finally, please upload your final report to the learning platform by December fourteenth.

head: From: Capstone Committee <capstone@eng.university.edu.tw>
To: Senior Project Teams
Subject: Booth Assignments and Equipment Requests for the Showcase
passage: Booth assignments for the Capstone Showcase on December 9 are now posted on the department website. Each booth includes one table, two chairs, and a poster board. If your project requires additional equipment, such as a monitor, extension cords, or a Wi-Fi connection, please fill out the online request form by December 3. Requests received after this date cannot be guaranteed.

Because the hall has a limited number of power outlets, teams whose projects run on batteries are encouraged to bring fully charged backup batteries. Heating devices and anything that produces smoke are strictly prohibited.
If you would like to swap booths with another team, both teams must agree and notify the committee in writing. We look forward to seeing the results of your hard work.

passage: For years, capstone projects at our university were seen mainly as a graduation requirement, something students completed, presented once, and then forgot. That view is changing. At last year's Capstone Showcase, more than forty companies sent representatives, nearly double the number from three years ago, and several student teams received offers to continue developing their projects with industry support.

One example is a team from the Department of Mechanical Engineering that designed a low-cost device to help elderly people stand up from a chair. After the showcase, a medical equipment company invited the team to test the device in two nursing homes in Taichung. "We built it for a class," said team leader Chen Yu-ting, "but now real people are using it, and their feedback is shaping every new version."

Professor Wang Mei-hua, who coordinates the program, believes this shift benefits students in several ways. "When students know that engineers from real companies will see their work, they take user needs much more seriously," she explained. "They also learn to explain technical ideas to people outside their field, which is a skill employers value highly."

However, not everyone sees only advantages. Some faculty members worry that projects may become too focused on commercial success. "A capstone should give students room to experiment and even fail," said Professor Lee Chih-ming. "If every project has to be marketable, students may avoid risky but creative ideas." To address this concern, the department now gives a separate award for the most innovative project, regardless of its business potential.
This year's showcase will take place on December 9, and organizers expect a record number of visitors.
